In eighteen fifty-nine, the night sky turned red over Cuba, and telegraph wires started sparking across two continents at the same time. On September first, astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots when two blinding white flashes erupted from the Sun's surface. It was the first solar flare anyone had ever recorded. About seventeen hours later, a giant magnetic storm slammed into Earth. Auroras glowed so brightly that people in the northeastern United States could read newspapers by their light at midnight. Telegraph operators got electric shocks, and some lines kept sending messages for two hours with their batteries completely disconnected. Scientists call it the Carrington Event, the strongest geomagnetic storm on record. A storm like that today could damage satellites and power grids.
